meaning: The joining of sperm and egg contributions to form a zygote.
example: A sperm and an oocyte contribute their chromosome sets in an oviduct.
importantDistinction: Fertilization precedes implantation; these are different events in different locations.
whatItDoes: A sperm and an oocyte contribute their chromosome sets in an oviduct.
feature: A sperm and an oocyte contribute their chromosome sets in an oviduct.
confusion: Fertilization precedes implantation; these are different events in different locations.

meaning: The single diploid cell formed by fertilization.
example: The first cell contains 23 chromosomes from each gamete.
importantDistinction: A zygote is a cell, not a ball of many cells.
whatItDoes: The first cell contains 23 chromosomes from each gamete.
feature: The first cell contains 23 chromosomes from each gamete.
confusion: A zygote is a cell, not a ball of many cells.

meaning: Having one set of chromosomes, represented by n.
example: A typical human gamete contains 23 chromosomes.
importantDistinction: One set still contains many different chromosomes.
whatItDoes: A typical human gamete contains 23 chromosomes.
feature: A typical human gamete contains 23 chromosomes.
confusion: One set still contains many different chromosomes.

meaning: Having two sets of chromosomes, represented by 2n.
example: A typical human zygote contains 46 chromosomes in two sets.
importantDistinction: Two sets does not mean the chromosomes have already been copied for division.
whatItDoes: A typical human zygote contains 46 chromosomes in two sets.
feature: A typical human zygote contains 46 chromosomes in two sets.
confusion: Two sets does not mean the chromosomes have already been copied for division.

meaning: Early mitotic divisions that increase cell number with little increase in the conceptus’s total size.
example: A two-cell stage becomes four smaller cells within the original overall boundary.
importantDistinction: More cells during cleavage does not mean the whole structure becomes proportionately larger.
whatItDoes: A two-cell stage becomes four smaller cells within the original overall boundary.
feature: A two-cell stage becomes four smaller cells within the original overall boundary.
confusion: More cells during cleavage does not mean the whole structure becomes proportionately larger.

meaning: A compact, solid ball of early embryonic cells.
example: An early compact ball contains roughly sixteen cells and no large internal cavity.
importantDistinction: A morula is different from the later fluid-filled blastocyst.
whatItDoes: An early compact ball contains roughly sixteen cells and no large internal cavity.
feature: An early compact ball contains roughly sixteen cells and no large internal cavity.
confusion: A morula is different from the later fluid-filled blastocyst.

meaning: An early developmental structure with a fluid-filled cavity, inner cell mass and outer trophoblast.
example: A hollow early structure has a cell cluster on one side and an outer cell layer.
importantDistinction: Different cell regions have different developmental contributions.
whatItDoes: A hollow early structure has a cell cluster on one side and an outer cell layer.
feature: A hollow early structure has a cell cluster on one side and an outer cell layer.
confusion: Different cell regions have different developmental contributions.

meaning: Attachment and embedding of the blastocyst in the uterine endometrium.
example: A blastocyst begins embedding in the uterine lining near the end of the first week after fertilization.
importantDistinction: The attaching stage is a blastocyst, not an unchanged one-cell zygote.
whatItDoes: A blastocyst begins embedding in the uterine lining near the end of the first week after fertilization.
feature: A blastocyst begins embedding in the uterine lining near the end of the first week after fertilization.
confusion: The attaching stage is a blastocyst, not an unchanged one-cell zygote.

meaning: A hormone released by developing trophoblast-derived tissue that helps maintain the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.
example: An early pregnancy signal keeps a temporary ovarian gland active.
importantDistinction: hCG acts on the corpus luteum; progesterone is a major signal supporting the endometrium.
whatItDoes: An early pregnancy signal keeps a temporary ovarian gland active.
feature: An early pregnancy signal keeps a temporary ovarian gland active.
confusion: hCG acts on the corpus luteum; progesterone is a major signal supporting the endometrium.

meaning: The outer cell layer of the blastocyst that contributes to implantation and fetal support tissues.
example: Outer cells interact with the uterine lining and contribute to chorionic tissues.
importantDistinction: The trophoblast is not the inner cell mass.
whatItDoes: Outer cells interact with the uterine lining and contribute to chorionic tissues.
feature: Outer cells interact with the uterine lining and contribute to chorionic tissues.
confusion: The trophoblast is not the inner cell mass.

meaning: The temporary ovarian endocrine structure formed after ovulation.
example: Remaining follicular tissue continues releasing progesterone when supported by an early pregnancy signal.
importantDistinction: It is in the ovary, not inside the blastocyst.
whatItDoes: Remaining follicular tissue continues releasing progesterone when supported by an early pregnancy signal.
feature: Remaining follicular tissue continues releasing progesterone when supported by an early pregnancy signal.
confusion: It is in the ovary, not inside the blastocyst.

meaning: A hormone that helps maintain a supportive uterine lining during pregnancy.
example: Endometrial tissue remains supported instead of being shed as a normal menstrual period.
importantDistinction: A hormone must reach responsive target tissues to produce its effect.
whatItDoes: Endometrial tissue remains supported instead of being shed as a normal menstrual period.
feature: Endometrial tissue remains supported instead of being shed as a normal menstrual period.
confusion: A hormone must reach responsive target tissues to produce its effect.

meaning: The cell movements that establish three primary germ layers in the embryo.
example: An early embryonic disc is reorganized into outer, middle and inner tissue-forming layers.
importantDistinction: Gastrulation changes organization; it is not simply another name for cleavage.
whatItDoes: An early embryonic disc is reorganized into outer, middle and inner tissue-forming layers.
feature: An early embryonic disc is reorganized into outer, middle and inner tissue-forming layers.
confusion: Gastrulation changes organization; it is not simply another name for cleavage.

meaning: The germ layer that gives rise to the nervous system and epidermis, among other tissues.
example: Neural tissue and the outer skin layer develop from the same primary germ layer.
importantDistinction: Epidermis is not the same as every tissue in the skin.
whatItDoes: Neural tissue and the outer skin layer develop from the same primary germ layer.
feature: Neural tissue and the outer skin layer develop from the same primary germ layer.
confusion: Epidermis is not the same as every tissue in the skin.

meaning: The middle germ layer that contributes to muscle, skeleton, blood and many reproductive and urinary structures.
example: Developing muscle and circulatory tissues share a middle-layer origin.
importantDistinction: Whole organs often contain tissues from more than one germ layer.
whatItDoes: Developing muscle and circulatory tissues share a middle-layer origin.
feature: Developing muscle and circulatory tissues share a middle-layer origin.
confusion: Whole organs often contain tissues from more than one germ layer.

meaning: The germ layer that forms much of the epithelial lining of digestive and respiratory passages and parts of associated glands.
example: The epithelial lining of the gut develops from the inner germ layer.
importantDistinction: The gut wall also contains muscle and connective tissues from other layers.
whatItDoes: The epithelial lining of the gut develops from the inner germ layer.
feature: The epithelial lining of the gut develops from the inner germ layer.
confusion: The gut wall also contains muscle and connective tissues from other layers.

meaning: The membrane enclosing the fluid-filled amniotic cavity around the developing embryo or fetus.
example: A thin membrane surrounds the space in which the fetus moves.
importantDistinction: The amnion is the membrane; amniotic fluid is its contents.
whatItDoes: A thin membrane surrounds the space in which the fetus moves.
feature: A thin membrane surrounds the space in which the fetus moves.
confusion: The amnion is the membrane; amniotic fluid is its contents.

meaning: The outer extraembryonic membrane whose villi contribute to the fetal portion of the placenta.
example: Finger-like projections from an outer membrane increase contact area for exchange.
importantDistinction: Chorion and amnion are distinct membranes.
whatItDoes: Finger-like projections from an outer membrane increase contact area for exchange.
feature: Finger-like projections from an outer membrane increase contact area for exchange.
confusion: Chorion and amnion are distinct membranes.

meaning: An early extraembryonic structure involved in early blood-cell formation and development, without a large food-yolk store in humans.
example: An early sac beneath the embryo contributes to early blood-cell formation.
importantDistinction: The human yolk sac is not a large nutrient-filled egg yolk.
whatItDoes: An early sac beneath the embryo contributes to early blood-cell formation.
feature: An early sac beneath the embryo contributes to early blood-cell formation.
confusion: The human yolk sac is not a large nutrient-filled egg yolk.

meaning: An early extraembryonic outgrowth associated with the connecting stalk and development of the bladder connection.
example: A small outgrowth extends into the stalk of an early embryo.
importantDistinction: In humans it is not a large waste-storage sac like that in some egg-laying animals.
whatItDoes: A small outgrowth extends into the stalk of an early embryo.
feature: A small outgrowth extends into the stalk of an early embryo.
confusion: In humans it is not a large waste-storage sac like that in some egg-laying animals.

meaning: The development of specialized cell structures and functions.
example: Cells become specialized for contraction or electrical signalling.
importantDistinction: Specialization generally involves different gene expression, not a completely different genome.
whatItDoes: Cells become specialized for contraction or electrical signalling.
feature: Cells become specialized for contraction or electrical signalling.
confusion: Specialization generally involves different gene expression, not a completely different genome.

meaning: The development of the shape and organization of body structures.
example: An initially flatter embryonic structure folds into a three-dimensional body form.
importantDistinction: Changes in shape and arrangement are distinct from simply making more cells.
whatItDoes: An initially flatter embryonic structure folds into a three-dimensional body form.
feature: An initially flatter embryonic structure folds into a three-dimensional body form.
confusion: Changes in shape and arrangement are distinct from simply making more cells.

meaning: The formation of early organ structures from developing tissues.
example: Early heart, limb and nervous-system structures are established during embryonic development.
importantDistinction: An organ’s early appearance does not mean it is mature.
whatItDoes: Early heart, limb and nervous-system structures are established during embryonic development.
feature: Early heart, limb and nervous-system structures are established during embryonic development.
confusion: An organ’s early appearance does not mean it is mature.

meaning: Formation of the neural tube from specialized ectoderm.
example: Neural folds move toward one another and enclose a tube.
importantDistinction: The neural tube gives rise to the brain and spinal cord.
whatItDoes: Neural folds move toward one another and enclose a tube.
feature: Neural folds move toward one another and enclose a tube.
confusion: The neural tube gives rise to the brain and spinal cord.

meaning: An organ formed from fetal and maternal contributions that supports exchange and hormone production during pregnancy.
example: A branching fetal exchange surface lies close to maternal blood in the uterus.
importantDistinction: The two blood supplies are normally separated by tissue barriers.
whatItDoes: A branching fetal exchange surface lies close to maternal blood in the uterus.
feature: A branching fetal exchange surface lies close to maternal blood in the uterus.
confusion: The two blood supplies are normally separated by tissue barriers.

meaning: A projection containing fetal tissues and capillaries that increases placental exchange area.
example: Numerous small projections bring fetal capillaries close to maternal blood.
importantDistinction: A large surface area supports exchange without requiring bulk blood mixing.
whatItDoes: Numerous small projections bring fetal capillaries close to maternal blood.
feature: Numerous small projections bring fetal capillaries close to maternal blood.
confusion: A large surface area supports exchange without requiring bulk blood mixing.

meaning: A vessel carrying blood from the fetus toward the placenta.
example: Fetal blood travels away from the fetal heart to the exchange organ.
importantDistinction: Arteries are named by direction away from the heart, not by oxygen content.
whatItDoes: Fetal blood travels away from the fetal heart to the exchange organ.
feature: Fetal blood travels away from the fetal heart to the exchange organ.
confusion: Arteries are named by direction away from the heart, not by oxygen content.

meaning: The vessel carrying blood from the placenta toward the fetus.
example: Blood carrying exchanged oxygen and nutrients returns to the fetus.
importantDistinction: A vein can carry relatively oxygen-rich blood.
whatItDoes: Blood carrying exchanged oxygen and nutrients returns to the fetus.
feature: Blood carrying exchanged oxygen and nutrients returns to the fetus.
confusion: A vein can carry relatively oxygen-rich blood.

meaning: The early period through eight weeks after fertilization, during which the body plan and basic organ structures are established.
example: Early organ formation is taking place before the fetal period begins.
importantDistinction: Some classifications name the first two weeks separately as pre-embryonic.
whatItDoes: Early organ formation is taking place before the fetal period begins.
feature: Early organ formation is taking place before the fetal period begins.
confusion: Some classifications name the first two weeks separately as pre-embryonic.

meaning: The period from the beginning of week nine after fertilization until birth, emphasizing growth and maturation.
example: Established organ systems continue to grow and become more functional.
importantDistinction: The fetal period does not end at week twelve.
whatItDoes: Established organ systems continue to grow and become more functional.
feature: Established organ systems continue to grow and become more functional.
confusion: The fetal period does not end at week twelve.

meaning: Pregnancy age conventionally counted from the first day of the last menstrual period.
example: A pregnancy age is counted from a menstrual date rather than directly from fertilization.
importantDistinction: It is commonly about two weeks ahead of age from fertilization in an illustrative cycle.
whatItDoes: A pregnancy age is counted from a menstrual date rather than directly from fertilization.
feature: A pregnancy age is counted from a menstrual date rather than directly from fertilization.
confusion: It is commonly about two weeks ahead of age from fertilization in an illustrative cycle.

meaning: An environmental agent capable of disturbing prenatal development.
example: Alcohol exposure can disrupt developmental processes.
importantDistinction: Risk depends on exposure timing, amount and susceptibility; not every exposure produces the same outcome.
whatItDoes: Alcohol exposure can disrupt developmental processes.
feature: Alcohol exposure can disrupt developmental processes.
confusion: Risk depends on exposure timing, amount and susceptibility; not every exposure produces the same outcome.

meaning: The process of labour and birth.
example: Labour progresses through cervical dilation, delivery of the baby and delivery of the placenta.
importantDistinction: Birth of the baby is not the completion of placental delivery.
whatItDoes: Labour progresses through cervical dilation, delivery of the baby and delivery of the placenta.
feature: Labour progresses through cervical dilation, delivery of the baby and delivery of the placenta.
confusion: Birth of the baby is not the completion of placental delivery.

meaning: Widening of the cervix during labour.
example: The cervical opening becomes wider as labour progresses.
importantDistinction: Dilation is not the same as expulsion of the placenta.
whatItDoes: The cervical opening becomes wider as labour progresses.
feature: The cervical opening becomes wider as labour progresses.
confusion: Dilation is not the same as expulsion of the placenta.

meaning: A hormone made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary that supports uterine contractions and milk ejection.
example: A neural signal leads to a hormone release that strengthens uterine contraction.
importantDistinction: Its role in milk ejection differs from prolactin’s role in milk production.
whatItDoes: A neural signal leads to a hormone release that strengthens uterine contraction.
feature: A neural signal leads to a hormone release that strengthens uterine contraction.
confusion: Its role in milk ejection differs from prolactin’s role in milk production.

meaning: A response that reinforces the initiating change.
example: Stronger contractions increase cervical stretch, leading to further contraction-promoting signalling.
importantDistinction: Positive refers to reinforcement, not whether an outcome is desirable.
whatItDoes: Stronger contractions increase cervical stretch, leading to further contraction-promoting signalling.
feature: Stronger contractions increase cervical stretch, leading to further contraction-promoting signalling.
confusion: Positive refers to reinforcement, not whether an outcome is desirable.

meaning: Milk production and secretion by the mammary glands.
example: Mammary tissue provides milk after birth.
importantDistinction: Production and ejection involve different main hormonal actions.
whatItDoes: Mammary tissue provides milk after birth.
feature: Mammary tissue provides milk after birth.
confusion: Production and ejection involve different main hormonal actions.

meaning: An anterior-pituitary hormone that stimulates milk production.
example: Mammary secretory cells increase synthesis of milk components.
importantDistinction: Prolactin production support is distinct from oxytocin-driven ejection.
whatItDoes: Mammary secretory cells increase synthesis of milk components.
feature: Mammary secretory cells increase synthesis of milk components.
confusion: Prolactin production support is distinct from oxytocin-driven ejection.

meaning: Movement of milk toward the nipple through contraction of cells around mammary secretory structures.
example: Milk already present is moved into the duct system during let-down.
importantDistinction: Ejection does not mean new milk has just been synthesized.
whatItDoes: Milk already present is moved into the duct system during let-down.
feature: Milk already present is moved into the duct system during let-down.
confusion: Ejection does not mean new milk has just been synthesized.

meaning: A neural and hormonal response initiated by sensory stimulation during feeding.
example: Sensory information from the nipple leads to central hormone responses.
importantDistinction: Sensory information travels through nerves; hormones act through blood.
whatItDoes: Sensory information from the nipple leads to central hormone responses.
feature: Sensory information from the nipple leads to central hormone responses.
confusion: Sensory information travels through nerves; hormones act through blood.

meaning: A process in which eggs and sperm are brought together outside the body and resulting embryos may be transferred to the uterus.
example: Fertilization takes place in a laboratory before an embryo is transferred.
importantDistinction: Embryo transfer does not guarantee implantation or birth.
whatItDoes: Fertilization takes place in a laboratory before an embryo is transferred.
feature: Fertilization takes place in a laboratory before an embryo is transferred.
confusion: Embryo transfer does not guarantee implantation or birth.

meaning: Placement of sperm in the reproductive tract to support the chance of fertilization.
example: Prepared sperm are introduced into the reproductive tract without intercourse.
importantDistinction: Fertilization still occurs inside the reproductive tract, unlike laboratory fertilization in IVF.
whatItDoes: Prepared sperm are introduced into the reproductive tract without intercourse.
feature: Prepared sperm are introduced into the reproductive tract without intercourse.
confusion: Fertilization still occurs inside the reproductive tract, unlike laboratory fertilization in IVF.

meaning: Use of hormone-like signals to reduce the chance of pregnancy through effects such as suppressing ovulation or changing cervical mucus.
example: A method alters reproductive feedback and/or conditions for sperm passage.
importantDistinction: Different hormonal methods do not all act identically.
whatItDoes: A method alters reproductive feedback and/or conditions for sperm passage.
feature: A method alters reproductive feedback and/or conditions for sperm passage.
confusion: Different hormonal methods do not all act identically.

meaning: A procedure that interrupts sperm transport through the vasa deferentia.
example: Sperm transport is interrupted while testes can still produce hormones.
importantDistinction: A transport interruption does not by itself stop testosterone production.
whatItDoes: Sperm transport is interrupted while testes can still produce hormones.
feature: Sperm transport is interrupted while testes can still produce hormones.
confusion: A transport interruption does not by itself stop testosterone production.
